proposals.before:
Corollary 7.12

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category admitting a small generating subcategory \(C\), and such that every object of \(E\) is the source of a monomorphism into an object injective of \(E\). Suppose moreover that for every \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the sum \(T \sqcup T\) in \(E\) is representable, and that every morphism with source \(T \sqcup T\) factors as an epimorphism effective followed by a monomorphism. Then \(E\) admits a full cogenerating subcategory \(D\). More precisely, one can take \(D\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{ob}\, D \leq \prod_{T,T'\in\mathrm{ob}\, C} 2^{\mathrm{card}(\mathrm{Hom}(T',T\sqcup T))^2}\).

Proposition 4.7

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(\widetilde{C}\) the category of sheaves on \(C\) for the canonical topology, \(\varepsilon_C : C \to \widetilde{C}\) the canonical functor (4.4.0), \(R \rightrightarrows X\) an equivalence relation in \(C\) admitting a cokernel \(Y\) in \(C\). Let \(\pi : X \to Y\) be the morphism canonical and suppose it squarable. Consider then the following properties:

i) \(\varepsilon_C(Y)\) is the quotient of the equivalence relation \(\varepsilon_C(R) \rightrightarrows \varepsilon_C(X)\).

ii) The equivalence relation \(R \rightrightarrows X\) is universal effective (cf. n° 7).

One has ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). When \(C\) possesses a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topology less fine than the canonical topology, one has i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii).

proposals.before:
Definition 5.2

1) A morphism \(f : H \to K\) satisfying the three conditions equivalent of 5.1 is called a covering morphism. A family of morphisms \(f_i : H_i \to K\), \(i \in I\), with the same target is said to be covering if the corresponding morphism \(f : \coprod_i H_i \to K\) is covering.

2) A morphism \(f : H \to K\) is said to be bicovering if it is covering and if the morphism diagonal \(H \to H \times_K H\) is covering. A family \(f_i : H_i \to K\), \(i \in I\), with the same target is said to be bicovering if the corresponding morphism \(f : \coprod_i H_i \to K\) is bicovering.

proposals.before:
Proposition 5.4

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site. There exists on \(\widehat{C}\) a topology (evidently unique) such that a family \(H_i \to K\) of arrows of \(\widehat{C}\) with the same target is covering for this topology if and only if it is covering in the sense of 5.2. It is also the topology the least fine on \(\widehat{C}\) among the topologies \(T\) having the following properties:

a) \(T\) is finer than the canonical topology of \(\widehat{C}\) (i.e. every family epimorphic of \(\widehat{C}\) is covering for \(T\)).

b) Every covering family in \(C\) is covering in \(\widehat{C}\).

proposals.before: Proof. We shall limit ourselves to giving indications. We leave to the reader the task of showing that the covering families in the sense of 5.2 are the covering families of a topology \(T_C\) on \(\widehat{C}\) (one uses 4.1). The covering families of the canonical topology on \(\widehat{C}\) are the epimorphic families on \(\widehat{C}\) (2.6 and I 3.1). Since \(a\) commutes with inductive limits (4.1), the topology \(T_C\) is finer than the canonical topology of \(\widehat{C}\). Moreover the covering families of \(C\) are covering families of \(T_C\) (5.1). If, then, \(T'\) denotes the least fine of the topologies of \(\widehat{C}\) possessing the properties a) and b), \(T_C\) is finer than \(T'\). Let \((f_i : H_i \to K)\), \(i \in I\), be a covering family of \(T_C\). Let us show that \((f_i, i \in I)\) is a family covering of \(T'\). Let \(s_i : H_i \to H = \coprod H_i\) be the canonical monomorphisms and \(f = (f_i, i \in I) : H = \coprod_i H_i \to K\) the morphism defined by the \(f_i\). The family of the \(s_i\) is covering for \(T'\). To show that \((f_i, i \in I)\) is a covering family of \(T'\), it therefore suffices to show, by virtue of axiom (T2) of topologies, that the morphism \(f : H \to K\) is covering for \(T'\). There exists an epimorphic family of \(\widehat{C}\), \(u_\lambda : X_\lambda \to K\), \(\lambda \in \Lambda\), \(X_\lambda \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\) (I 3.4). To show that \(f : H \to K\) is covering for \(T'\), it therefore suffices, by virtue of axiom (T 2) of topologies, to show that for every \(\lambda \in \Lambda\), the morphism \(\mathrm{pr}_2 : H \times_K X_\lambda \to X_\lambda\) is covering for \(T'\). Let then \(v_j : Y_j \to H \times_K X_\lambda\), \(j \in J\), \(Y_j \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), be an epimorphic family of \(\widehat{C}\). The family \((\mathrm{pr}_2 \circ v_j, j \in J)\) is covering for \(T_C\). It is therefore a covering family of \(C\) (5.1). It is therefore a covering family of \(T'\). Consequently the sieve generated by \(\mathrm{pr}_2 : H \times_K X_\lambda \to X_\lambda\) contains a sieve covering for \(T'\). It is therefore covering for \(T'\) and consequently \(\mathrm{pr}_2 : H \times_K X_\lambda \to X_\lambda\) is covering, q.e.d.

proposals.before:
Remark 5.4.1

The proof of 5.4 shows in fact that every topology \(T'\) on \(\widehat{C}\), finer than the canonical topology of \(\widehat{C}\), is the least fine of the topologies \(T\) on \(\widehat{C}\) that possess the following properties:

a) \(T\) is finer than the canonical topology of \(\widehat{C}\).

b) Every family covering for \(T'\) of the form \(u_i : X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), where \(X\) and the \(X_i\) are objects of \(C\), is covering for \(T\).

In particular, every topology \(T'\) on \(\widehat{C}\), finer than the canonical topology, is uniquely determined by the families \(u_i : X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), \(X_i\) and \(X\) objects of \(C\), that are covering for \(T'\).

proposals.before:
Proposition 1.2

Let \(C\) be a small site, \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The functor \(u\) is continuous.

  2. ii)

    For every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\) covering \(X\), the morphism \(u_! R \to u(X)\) is bicovering in \(\widehat{C}'\) (II 5.2 and I 5.1).(∗)

  3. iii)

    For every bicovering family \(H_i \to K\), \(i \in I\), of \(\widehat{C}\), the family of the \(u_! H_i \to u_! K\), \(i \in I\), is bicovering in \(\widehat{C}'\).

  4. iv)

    There exists a functor \(u^s : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}'\), commuting with inductive limits and "extending \(u\)", i.e. such that the diagram of canonical functors \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{\varepsilon_C} & C' \ar[d]^-{\varepsilon_{C'}} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{u^s} & \widetilde{C}' } \] is commutative up to isomorphism.

Moreover, when \(C\) is no longer necessarily a small site, but a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, we always have i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) iv) and the functor \(u^s\) of iv) is necessarily a left adjoint of the functor \(u_s : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\), and is consequently determined up to unique isomorphism.

proposals.before:
Proposition 2.2

Let \(C\) be a small site, \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. We denote by \(\widehat{u}_* : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C}'\) the right adjoint functor of the functor \(F \mapsto F \circ u = \widehat{u}^* F\) (I 5.1). The functor \(u\) is cocontinuous if and only if for every sheaf \(G\) on \(C\), \(\widehat{u}_* G\) is a sheaf on \(C'\).

Proposition 2.2

Let \(C\) be a small site, \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor between the underlying categories. We denote by \(\widehat{u}_* : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C}'\) the right adjoint to the functor \(F \mapsto F \circ u = \widehat{u}^* F\) (I 5.1). The functor \(u\) is cocontinuous if and only if for every sheaf \(G\) on \(C\), \(\widehat{u}_* G\) is a sheaf on \(C'\).

proposals.before: Proof. The condition is sufficient. Suppose that for every sheaf \(G\) on \(C\), the presheaf \(\widehat{u}_* G\) is a sheaf. Let \(Y\) be an object of \(C\) and \(R \hookrightarrow u(Y)\) a covering sieve. We have an isomorphism \(\mathrm{Hom}(u(Y), \widehat{u}_* G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(R, \widehat{u}_* G)\), whence by adjunction (I 5.1) an iso- morphism \(\mathrm{Hom}(\widehat{u}^* \circ u(Y), G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(\widehat{u}^* R, G)\). We deduce (II 5.3) that the morphism \(\widehat{u}^* R \to \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) is bicovering. But the functor \(\widehat{u}^*\) commutes with projective limits and consequently the morphism \(\widehat{u}^* R \to \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) is a monomorphism. It is therefore a covering monomorphism. On the other hand we have a canonical morphism \(Y \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) deduced from the adjunction morphism \(\mathrm{id}_C \to \widehat{u}^* u\), (I 5.4 3)). Let us then make the base change \(Y \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\). We obtain a sieve covering \(Y\): \[ \widehat{u}^* R \times_{\widehat{u}^* u(Y)} Y \longrightarrow Y , \] and when one seeks the arrows \(Z \to Y\) which factor through this sieve, one obtains the sieve described by property (COC).

Proposition 2.3

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites and \(u : C \to C'\) a cocontinuous functor. We denote by \(u^* : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) the functor \(u^* = a \widehat{u}^* i'\), where \(a\) denotes the "associated sheaf" functor for \(C\), \(\widehat{u}^*\) the functor \(F \mapsto F \circ u\), \(i'\) the inclusion functor \(\widetilde{C}' \to \widehat{C}'\).

  1. 1)

    The functor \(u^*\) commutes with inductive limits and is exact.

  2. 2)

    We have a canonical isomorphism \(u^* a' \simeq a \widehat{u}^*\), where \(a'\) denotes the "associated sheaf" functor for \(\widehat{C}'\).

    Let \(\mathcal{V} \supset \mathcal{U}\) be a universe. We denote by \(u_{*\mathcal{U}} : \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \to \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{U}}\) (resp. \(u_{*\mathcal{V}} : \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \to \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{V}}\)) the right adjoint functor relative to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)) whose exis- tence is affirmed in 3). proposals.before:
Proposition 2.5

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites and \(C \overset{v}{\underset{u}{\rightleftarrows}} C'\) a pair of functors, where \(v\) is left adjoint of \(u\). The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The functor \(u\) is continuous.

  2. ii)

    The functor \(v\) is cocontinuous.

Moreover, under these equivalent conditions, we have canonical isomorphisms \(v_* \simeq u_s\), \(v^* \simeq u^s\). In particular, the functor \(u^s\) commutes with finite projective limits.

The converse follows from the existence of the commutative diagram 1.2 iv), taking into account the fact that the functors \(\varepsilon_C\) and \(\varepsilon_{C'}\) are fully faithful when the topologies are coarser than the canonical topology, q.e.d.

proposals.before: To say that \(u : F \to G\) is covering for a given topology \(T\) means that for every arrow \(X \to G\), with \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\), the corresponding arrow \(F \times_G X \to X\) is covering, or, equivalently, that the family of arrows \(X' \to X\) of \(C\) which factor through the preceding arrow is covering. The fact that there exists a coarsest topology among those for which the \(u_i : F_i \to G_i\) are covering thus follows from I 1.1.6, whence the non-resp. assertion of 3.6.1. The resp. assertion is deduced from it, upon recalling that a morphism \(u : F \to G\) is bicovering if and only if the morphisms \(u : F \to G\) and \(\mathrm{diag}_u : F \to F \times_G F\) are covering.

proposals.before: The introduction of classifying topoi (via the "big sites") has over classifying spaces the advantage of providing a richer theory, since they furnish in particular invariants cohomological useful for coefficients more general than constant or locally constant coefficients. Moreover, the definition considered here adapts in an obvious way to the other usual contexts: differentiable manifolds, analytic manifolds or spaces (real or complex, as one wishes), schemes. This point of view makes it possible in particular to establish the link between the study of characteristic classes from the traditional point of view and from the "arithmetic" point of view, by regarding the "classical groups" as arising from schemes defined over the ring of integers; cf. [7] for indications in this direction. Likewise, the general results of J. GIRAUD [3] on the classification of extensions of Groups, developed in the very general and very flexible framework of topoi, can, thanks to the "big topoi", be specialized into results on the classification of extensions of topological groups, or of real or complex Lie groups, which did not seem to be much known to topologists except in the case of extensions with abelian kernel [11].

Exercise 2.7.5

Define for a topos \(E\) the notion of connectedness, of local connectedness(∗), of simple connectedness and of local simple connectedness. Define the notion of constant and locally constant object of \(E\) (cf. IX 2.0). Let \(f : E' \to E\) be a morphism of topoi (3.1), with \(E'\) simply connected (for example \(E'\) the punctual topos (2.2)), and \(E\) connected and locally connected. proposals.before: The existence of the functor \(j_{X!}\) follows from III 1.7. Since \(j_{X!}\) is a left adjoint, it commutes with inductive limits (I 2). One knows then that \(E_{/X}\) is equivalent to the category of presheaves on \(C_{/X}\), and that, modulo this equivalence, the functor \(j_X^* : E \to E_{/X}\) is none other than the composition with the forgetful functor \(C_{/X} \to C\) (I 5.11). Lemma 2.14.1

Let \(X\) be a geometrically unibranch scheme (for example normal), \(i : U \longrightarrow X\) a quasi-compact open immersion. proposals.before:
Exercise 4.16

We say that a topos \(E\) is generated by its opens if the opens of \(E\) (i.e. the subobjects of the final object \(e\) of \(E\)) form a generating family (I 7). Such a topos possesses the property following:

(P) Every epimorphic family \(X_i \longrightarrow X\), \(i \in I\), is dominated by a family epimorphic \(U_j \longrightarrow X\), \(j \in J\), where the \(U_j \longrightarrow X\) are monomorphisms.

a) Do there exist topoi that possess property (P) and that are not generated by their opens? The topoi associated to topological spaces are generated by their opens. If \(E\) is generated by its opens (resp. enjoys (P)), then for every object \(X\) of \(E\), \(E_{/X}\) is generated by its opens (resp. enjoys (P)). Every subtopos of a topos generated by its opens is generated by its opens. Property (P) is not a property of local character.

b) Let \(E\) be a topos and \(\operatorname{Ouv}(E)\) the category of opens of \(E\) equipped with the topology induced. The inclusion functor \(\operatorname{Ouv}(E) \longrightarrow E\) is a morphism of sites, whence a morphism of topoi \(\Pi : E \longrightarrow \widetilde{\operatorname{Ouv}(E)}\). The functor \(\Pi^*\) is fully faithful. The morphism \(\Pi\) possesses, with respect to the 2-category of topoi generated by their opens, a universal property which the reader will make explicit.

c) Let \(E\) be a topos generated by its opens and \(\operatorname{Point}(E)\) the set of points up to isomorphism of \(E\). Show that \(\operatorname{Point}(E)\) is small. Put a topology on \(\operatorname{Point}(E)\) and define a morphism \(\operatorname{Top}(\operatorname{Point}(E)) \longrightarrow \widetilde{\operatorname{Ouv}(E)}\) making \(\operatorname{Top}(\operatorname{Point}(E))\) a subtopos of \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Ouv}(E)}\). For every topological space \(X\), show that every morphism from \(\operatorname{Top}(X)\) to \(E\) yields a morphism from \(\operatorname{Top}(X)\) to \(\operatorname{Top}(\operatorname{Point}(E))\). Show that a topos generated by its opens is equivalent to a topos \(\operatorname{Top}(X)\) (\(X\) a topological space) if and only if it has enough points. Show that there exist topoi generated by their opens that are not equivalent to topoi \(\operatorname{Top}(X)\) where \(X\) is a topological space.

d) Let \(E\) be a topos possessing property (P). In order for an abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(E\) to be flasque, it is necessary and sufficient that for every monomorphism \(X \hookrightarrow Y\), the homomorphism \(F(Y) \longrightarrow F(X)\) be surjective.

e) Let \(E\) be a topos possessing property (P). Show that the property, for a sheaf \(F\), of being flasque is a property of local nature.

f) Let \(E\) be a topos generated by its opens and \(e\) the final object of \(E\). In order for an abelian sheaf \(F\) to be flasque, it is necessary and sufficient that for every open \(U\) of \(e\), the canonical morphism \(F(e) \longrightarrow F(U)\) be surjective.

Setting \[ \mathcal{A} = \varinjlim_i \mathcal{A}_i , \] one may take \[ X = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{A} . \] Moreover, denoting by esp \(S\) the topological space underlying a scheme \(S\), one shows (EGA IV 8...) that the canonical map \[ \mathrm{esp}\, X \to \varprojlim \mathrm{esp}(X_i) \] is a homeomorphism and that the canonical homomorphism of sheaves of rings \[ \varinjlim_i \gamma_i^{-1}(\mathcal{O}_{X_i}) \to \mathcal{O}_X \] is bijective, where \(\gamma_i : X \to X_i\) is the canonical continuous map.

proposals.before: We saw in N° 4 how one associates, to every geometric point \(\xi\) of the scheme \(X\), a strictly local \(X\)-scheme \[ \overline{X}(\xi) = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} , \] depending, in fact, only on the geometric point above the image \(x\) of \(\xi\) defined by the separable closure \(\overline{k(x)}\) of \(k(x)\) in \(\Omega = k(\xi)\). We shall often restrict ourselves in what follows to the geometric points \(\xi = \operatorname{Spec} \Omega\) that are algebraic separable over \(X\), i.e. such that \(\Omega\) is a separable closure of \(k(x)\), i.e. \(\xi = \bar{x}\). Let us call an \(X\)-scheme \(Z\) a strict localization of \(X\) if it is \(X\)-isomorphic to a scheme of the form \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\bar{x}}\); we thus see that \[ \xi \mapsto \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} = \overline{X}(\xi) \] is an equivalence from the category of geometric points that are algebraic separable over \(X\), with the category of \(X\)-schemes that are strict localizations of \(X\), when one takes as morphisms in both categories the isomorphisms alone.
proposals.after: We saw in N° 4 how one associates, to every geometric point \(\xi\) of the scheme \(X\), a strictly local \(X\)-scheme \[ \overline{X}(\xi) = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} , \] depending, in fact, only on the geometric point above the image \(x\) of \(\xi\) defined by the separable closure \(\overline{k(x)}\) of \(k(x)\) in \(\Omega = k(\xi)\). We shall often restrict ourselves in what follows to the geometric points \(\xi = \operatorname{Spec} \Omega\) that are separably algebraic over \(X\), i.e. such that \(\Omega\) is a separable closure of \(k(x)\), i.e. \(\xi = \bar{x}\). proposals.before: If \(E\) is a topos, recall (IV ) that one has called "stalk functor", or (by abuse of language) "point" of the topos \(E\), any morphism from the "final topos" (Ens) (isomorphic to the category of sheaves on a space reduced to a point!) into \(E\), i.e. any functor \[ \varphi = E \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] which commutes with arbitrary inductive limits, and with finite projective limits. It is appropriate to regard the set of stalk functors of \(E\) as the set of objects of a full subcategory of \(\operatorname{Hom}(E,(\mathrm{Ens}))\), called category of stalk functors of the topos \(E\), whose opposite is called category of points of \(E\), and denoted \(\operatorname{Pt}(E)\), cf. (IV 6.1).

It is appropriate to regard the set of fibre functors of \(E\) as the set of objects of a full subcategory of \(\operatorname{Hom}(E,(\mathrm{Ens}))\), called category of fibre functors of the topos \(E\), whose opposite is called category of points of \(E\), and denoted \(\operatorname{Pt}(E)\), cf. proposals.before: Let us first remark that if \(C\) is a site where finite \(\varprojlim\) are representable, \(\widetilde{C} = E\) the corresponding topos, then every stalk functor \(\varphi\) on \(E\) can be represented as a "filtered inductive limit" of functors of the form \[ \check{Y}(F) = F(\widetilde{Y}) = \operatorname{Hom}(\widetilde{Y}, F), \qquad Y \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C , \] (where \(\widetilde{Y}\) is the sheaf associated with \(Y\)), in the following way (∗). One considers the category \(C_{/\varphi}\) of pairs \((Y, \xi)\), with \(Y \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\), \(\xi \in \varphi(\widetilde{Y})\) (the morphisms being defined in the evident way), and one notes that one has an evident homomorphism \[ (*) \qquad \varinjlim_{(Y,\xi) \in C_{/\varphi}} \check{Y} \to \varphi \] by remarking that \[ \operatorname{Hom}(\varinjlim_{C_{/\varphi}} \check{Y}, \varphi) \simeq \varprojlim_{C_{/\varphi}} \operatorname{Hom}(\check{Y}, \varphi) \simeq \varprojlim_{C_{/\varphi}} \varphi(\widetilde{Y}) . \] Now one has a canonical element in \(\varprojlim_{C_{/\varphi}} \varphi(\widetilde{Y})\), by associating to every \((Y, \xi)\) the element \(\xi\) of \(\varphi(\widetilde{Y})\). Using the fact that finite \(\varprojlim\) exist in \(C\), and that the functor \(Y \mapsto \varphi(\widetilde{Y})\) commutes with them, we see that in \(C_{/\varphi}\) the finite \(\varprojlim\) exist; a fortiori \(C_{/\varphi}\) is filtered. Using that every sheaf \(F\) is an inductive limit of sheaves of the form \(\widetilde{Y}\), and using the fact that \(\varphi\) commutes with inductive limits, one easily concludes that the homomorphism of functors \((*)\) is bijective, and thus gives the announced representation.

a) When one is given a locally finite covering of \(Y\) by closed sets \(Y_i\), and one sets \(X = \coprod_i Y_i\) then the canonical morphism \(f : X \to Y\) is finite, and the spectral sequence 8.1 has an initial term which is made explicit as the cohomology of the complex defined by the \(H^q(Y_{i_0 \ldots i_p}, F|Y_{i_0 \ldots i_p})\), where \(Y_{i_0 \ldots i_p} = Y_{i_0} \cap \ldots \cap Y_{i_p}\). Lemma 6.2

Let \(C,C'\) be two abelian categories, \(T^\bullet = (T^i)\) and \(T'^\bullet = (T'^i)\) two cohomological functors from \(C\) to \(C'\), \(\varphi = (\varphi^i)\) a homomorphism of cohomological functors from \(T^\bullet\) to \(T'^\bullet\). Suppose \(T^\bullet\) and \(T'^\bullet\) are zero in degrees \(< 0\), and \(T^i\) effaceable for \(i > 0\). Let \(n\) be an integer. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. a) \(\varphi^i\) is an isomorphism for \(i \leq n\), a monomorphism for \(i = n + 1\).
  2. b) (If \(n \geq -1\)). The homomorphism \(\varphi^i\) is a monomorphism if \(i = 0\), and an epimorphism if \(i \leq n\).
  3. c) (If \(n \geq 0\)). The homomorphism \(\varphi^0\) is an isomorphism, and the \(T'^i\) are effa- ceable for \(0 < i \leq n\).

If these conditions are fulfilled, and if \(A \in \operatorname{Ob}(C)\), then \(\varphi^{n+1}(A) : T^{n+1}(A) \longrightarrow T'^{n+1}(A)\) is an epimorphism (hence an isomorphism) if and only if \(T'^{n+1}(A)\) is effaceable, i.e. if there exists a monomorphism \(A \to B\) such that the corresponding homomorphism \(T'^{n+1}(A) \to T'^{n+1}(B)\) is zero. If \(C' = (\mathrm{Ab})\) (the category of abelian groups), and if \(\xi \in T'^{n+1}(A)\), then \(\xi\) is in the image of \(T^{n+1}(A)\) if and only if \(\xi\) is effaceable, i.e. if there exists a monomorphism \(A \to B\) such that the image of \(\xi\) in \(T'^{n+1}(B)\) is zero.

proposals.before: Proof of 6.3. Let us first prove (i). The assertion is obvious if \(H^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i \leq n+1\), since then, by the degree properties imposed on \(T^\bullet\), \(T'^\bullet\), we will have \(T^i(K^\bullet) = T'^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i \leq n+1\). Let, on the other hand, \(m\) be an integer \(\geq 0\) such that \(H^i(K^\bullet) = 0\) for \(i < m\): such an integer exists, e.g. \(m = 0\) works. We proceed by descending induction on \(m\), the assertion being proved when \(m = n+2\). We therefore assume the assertion proved for the \(m' > m\), and prove it for \(m\). By the hypothesis on the degrees of \(K^\bullet\), \(K^\bullet\) is quasi-isomorphic to a complex in degrees \(\geq m\), so we may assume it to be in degrees \(\geq m\). There follows an exact sequence of complexes \[ 0 \longrightarrow H^m [-m] \longrightarrow K^\bullet \longrightarrow K'^\bullet \longrightarrow 0 , \] where \(H^m = H^m(K^\bullet)\), where the sign \([-m]\) indicates a shift by \(-m\) on the degrees of a complex, and where \(K'^\bullet\) is defined as the cokernel. Hence the cohomology objects of \(K'^\bullet\) are those of \(K^\bullet\) in degrees \(\geq m+1\), and are zero in degrees \(\leq m+1\); in particu- lar, we may apply the induction hypothesis to \(K'^\bullet\). The preceding exact sequence gives rise to a homomorphism of exact sequences \[ \xymatrix{ T^{i-1}(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{i-m}(H^m) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^i(K^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^i(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & T^{i+1-m}(H^m) \ar[d] \\ T'^{i-1}(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^{i-m}(H^m) \ar[r] & T'^i(K^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^i(K'^\bullet) \ar[r] & T'^{i+1-m}(H^m) } \] Then, taking \(i \leq n\) in the preceding diagram, and taking into account the induction hypothesis and \(m \geq 0\), we find that the vertical arrows around the middle vertical arrow are isomorphisms and a fortiori epi- morphisms, and that the right-hand vertical arrow is a monomorphism, so by the five lemma the middle vertical arrow is an epimorphism. Taking \(i \leq n+1\), we find likewise that the vertical arrows around the middle one are monomorphisms, the left-hand vertical arrow being an isomorphism and a fortiori an epimorphism, whence we conclude by the five lemma that the middle vertical arrow is a monomorphism, which establishes 6.3 (i).

proposals.before: To prove 6.6 (ii), we shall first prove the second asser- tion of 6.5 (i), namely that, granting condition a) of 6.5 (i), for every sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(X\), the functor \(P \mapsto h^*(P)\), from the category of torsors under \(F\) to the category of torsors under \(h^*(F)\), is faithful (resp. fully faithful), and hence, in the "resp." case, induces an injection on the \(H^1\). For this, if \(P\) and \(P'\) are two torsors under \(F\), let us denote by \(\underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_F(P,P')\) the sheaf of \(F\)-isomorphisms from \(P\) onto \(P'\). It is immediate that the formation of this sheaf commutes with every extension of the base, in particular with the ex- tension of the base by \(h\). (This is an assertion valid for every morphism of sites). Using the hypothesis on the effect of \(h^*\) on the \(H^0\) for the sheaf \(\underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_F(P,P')\), we find that the map \(\underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_F(P,P') \to \underline{\operatorname{Isom}}_F(h^*(P),h^*(P'))\) is injective (resp. bijective), which means that the functor \(P \mapsto h^*(P)\) is faithful (resp. fully faithful). (NB: in the category of torsors under a sheaf of groups, every homomorphism is an isomorphism). Let us note on the other hand that if \(F\) is a subsheaf of groups of a sheaf of groups \(G\), then giving a torsor \(P\) under \(F\) amounts to giving a torsor under \(G\) (namely the one deduced from \(P\) by extension \(F \to G\) of the structural Group), equipped with a section of \(Q/F\) (which is indeed interpreted as a "restriction of the structural Group" from \(G\) to \(F\)). This being said, with the notation of 6.6 (ii), since the image \(\eta\) of \(\xi\) in \(H^1(Y,h^*(G))\) comes from an element of \(H^1(X,G)\), the latter is defined by a torsor \(Q\) under \(G\), so that \(\eta\) is the class of the torsor \(h^*(Q)\) under \(h^*(G)\). The fact that \(\eta\) comes from a \(\xi \in H^1(Y,h^*(F))\) then makes explicit by saying that \(\xi\) is the class of the \(h^*(F)\)-tor- sor defined by \(h^*(Q)\) and a suitable section of \(h^*(Q)/h^*(F)\). Since the functor \(h^*\) is right exact, this last sheaf is none other than \(h^*(Q/F)\), and since \(h^*\) induces a bijection on the \(H^0\) of sheaves of sets, it follows that the section in question of \(h^*(Q)/h^*(F)\) comes from a section of \(Q/F\). This last then defines an \(F\)-torsor by restriction of the structural group, and the class of this torsor in \(H^1(X,F)\) evidently has \(\xi\) as image in \(H^1(Y,h^*(F))\). This proves 6.6 (ii) and completes the proof of 6.6.

proposals.before: Let us now prove 6.5, beginning with 6.5 (iii). Evidently a) implies a'), and the reverse implication is a special case of 6.2 (applied again to the case where \(C\) is the category of sheaves of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion on \(X\), and \(C'\) the category of sheaves of abelian groups), provided one proves the effa- ceability in \(C\) of the functors \(H^i(X,F)\) for \(i > 0\). This indeed offers no difficulty, but we can also dispense with proving this result, by noting that \(F\) is the filtered inductive limit of its subsheaves \(F_i\) for which there exists an integer \(n > 0\) annihilating \(F_i\) (IX 1.1). Then \(h^*(F)\) is the inductive limit of the \(h^*(F_i)\), and taking into account the commutation of cohomology with inductive limits (VII 3.3), resulting from the hypotheses of quasi-compactness and quasi-separation made on \(X\) and \(Y\) (which had not been used for 6.6), we reduce to proving condition a) for the \(F_i\), which brings us to the case where there exists an integer \(m > 0\) such that \(mF = 0\). We may evidently assume that the prime divisors of \(m\) are \(\in \mathbb{L}\), and we may then take for \(C\) the category of sheaves of \(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}\)-Modules on \(X\). But it is known that in this category, the functors \(H^i(X, - )\) for \(i \geq 1\) are effaceable ( ). This shows the equivalence of the conditions a) and a') of 6.5 (iii). On the other hand, applying a) to the direct image of a sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(F'\) on \(X'\), \(X'\) finite over \(X\), which is \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion thanks to IX 1.2 (v), 1.6 (iii), and using 6.4 and VIII 5.5, we find that the homomorphism \[ H^i(X',F') \longrightarrow H^i(Y',h'^*(F')) \] is an isomorphism for \(i \leq n\), a monomorphism for \(i = n+1\), whence a fortiori condition b). It remains to prove that this condition implies a'). For this, let us use the fact (IX 2.7.2) that every sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(F\) on \(X\) is the filtered inductive limit of constructible sheaves of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion; then the argument of passage to the limit already used shows that in a'), one may restrict to the case where \(F\) is constructible. By virtue of IX 2.14 there then exist a finite number of finite morphisms \(p_i : X'_i \to X\), constant sheaves of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(G_{X'_i}\) on the \(X'_i\), and an injective homomorphism \[ F \longrightarrow \prod_i p_{i*}(G_{X'_i}) \] This said, if \(n = -1\), i.e. when the desired conclusion reduces to the injectivity assertion for \(H^0(X,F) \to H^0(Y,h^*(F))\), one sees at once that in this question one may replace \(F\) by a sheaf \(G\) such that there exists a monomorphism \(F \to G\), and consequently one may replace \(F\) by the product of the \(p_{i*}(G_{X'_i})\). Taking 6.4 into account, we are thus reduced to proving the assertion by replacing \(h : Y \to X\) by \(h' : Y' \to X'\), and \(F\) by a constant sheaf on \(X'\) with value a finite ordinary group of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion \(G\). But \(G\) is isomorphic to a sum of groups of the form \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z}\), with \(\ell \in \mathbb{L}\). We are thus indeed reduced to verifying b). When \(n \geq 0\), one proceeds analogously. By induction on \(n\), we may assume the desired conclusion (and consequently a)) proved for the integer \(n-1\) instead of \(n\). Then using 6.6 (iii), one sees that one may again replace \(F\) by a sheaf \(G\) such that there exists a monomorphism \(F \to G\), and one will again take for \(G\) the sheaf \(p_*(G_{X'})\). Taking 6.4 into account and the vanishing of the \(R^i p_*\) \((i \geq 1)\) for a finite morphism (VIII 5.5), this brings us again to proving surjectivity for \(H^n\) by replacing \(h : Y \to X\) by an \(h' : Y' \to X'\), and \(F\) by a constant sheaf on \(X'\) with value a finite ordinary group of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion. Since injectivity is already secured thanks to the induction hypothesis and the implication a') \(\Longrightarrow\) a), we are again reduced, by dévissage on \(G\), to the case where \(G\) is of the form \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z}\), that is, to the case considered in condition b) of 6.5 (iii). Remark 6.7

(*) 1) Evidently, the arguments proving 6.5 and 6.6 are of a very general and essentially trivial nature, and it would be worthwhile to isolate them as abstract lemmas of the same water as 6.2 (the sheaves \(p_*(G_{X'})\) playing the role of cogenerators of the category \(C\) in which one works). We leave this pleasant exercise to the reader, and we merely point out that essentially the same statement could be given by looking at functors such as \(R^i f_*\) instead of the functors \(H^i\). The same remarks apply to 6.8, 6.11 below.

2) When \(X\) is noetherian, the arguments given show that in the statement of conditions b) and their variants in 6.5 (i) (ii) (iii), one may restrict oneself to taking \(X'\) integral; when \(X\) is universally Japanese, one may even take them integral and normal; this is also possible without the Japanese restriction on \(X\), provided one takes morphisms \(p : X' \to X\) that are integral instead of finite morphisms. We shall not make use of any of these variants in the remainder of the seminar.

3) The proof of 6.6 does not use the hypothesis of quasi-compact- ness and quasi-separation made on \(X\), and the same holds for the fact that in (i) (ii) (iii) condition a) implies the others, as well as for the equivalence of the conditions b), b'), b'') among themselves. Let us note on the other hand that form b) of the conditions 6.5 (i) shows that, for \(\mathbb{L} = \emptyset\), they are special cases (when \(X\) is quasi-compact quasi-separated) of 6.5 (iii), for \(n = -1\) resp. for \(n = 0\). This moreover remains true (restricting to the conditions in form a)) without the restriction stated on \(X\), as one sees easily thanks to the fact that for every sheaf of sets \(F\), and every prime number \(\ell\), one can find two abelian sheaves of \(\ell\)-torsion \(G\) and \(H\), and a homomorphism \(u : G \to H\) of the underlying sheaves of sets, such that \(F\) is isomorphic to the inverse image of the zero section (one will take for \(G\) the free \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell\mathbb{Z}\)-Module generated by \(F\), and for \(H\) the constant sheaf \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell\mathbb{Z}\) on \(X\)). The same argument shows that (without any restriction of quasi-compactness and quasi-separation) 6.5 (ii) a) (where it even suffices to take \(i = 0\)) implies the "resp." condition 6.5(i) a); this in turn allows, taking into account that this last already implies the injectivity of \(H^1(X,F) \to H^1(Y,h^*(F))\) for every sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(X\), to restrict oneself in the statement of 6.5 (ii) a) to requiring for \(i = 1\) the surjectivity of \(H^1(X,F) \to H^1(Y,h^*(F))\). Unfortunately, the case 6.5 (ii) cannot be viewed as a special case of 6.5 (iii), which often obliges us to repeat in the non-commutative case an argument already made essentially in the commutative case. Let us also note that, except for 6.10, the results that follow are stated so as to be valid without any hypothesis of quasi-compactness and quasi-separation.

Proposition 6.8

(Descent lemma). With the general notation of 6.5, suppose given in addition a morphism \(p : \bar X \to X\), let us denote by \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) the morphism deduced from \(h\) by the base change \(p\), and by \(p_Y : \bar Y \to Y\) the canonical morphism. We assume either that \(p\) is surjective, or that \(h\) is a closed immersion and that \(X = p(\bar X) \cup h(Y)\).

(i) Suppose that the morphism \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) satisfies the injec- tivity (resp. bijectivity) condition of 6.5 (i) a). In the "resp." case, suppose in addition that the base change morphism \[ (*) \qquad h^*(p_*(\bar F)) \longrightarrow p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F)) \] is injective for every sheaf of sets \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\). Then the morphism \(h : Y \to X\) also satisfies the injectivity (resp. bijec- tivity) condition of 6.5 (i) a).

(ii) Suppose that \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) satisfies the condition of 6.5 (ii) a), and that for every sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups \(\bar F\) on \(\bar X\), the base change morphism (*) is bijective. Then \(h : Y \to X\) also satisfies the condition of 6.5 (ii) a).

(iii) Suppose that \(\bar h : \bar Y \to \bar X\) satisfies the condition of 6.5 (iii) a), and that for every abelian sheaf \(\bar F\) of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion on \(\bar X\), the base change homomorphism \[ h^*(R^i p_*(\bar F)) \longrightarrow R^i p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F)) \] is bijective for \(i \leq n-1\), injective for \(i = n\) (where \(n\) is a given integer \(\geq 1\)). Then the morphism \(h : Y \to X\) also satisfies the condition of 6.5 (iii) a).

proposals.before: Proof of 6.8. In the case where \(p\) is not assumed surjective, but \(h\) is a closed immersion and \(X = p(\bar X) \cup h(Y)\), we consider the sum scheme \(\bar X'\) of \(\bar X\) and \(Y\), and the morphism \(p' : \bar X' \to X\) deduced from \(p\) and \(h\). Then \(p'\) is surjective; moreover one verifies trivially, in each of the three cases con- sidered (i) (ii) (iii), that the hypotheses made on the pair \((h,p)\) are still satisfied for the pair \((h,p')\). This therefore brings us to the case where \(p\) is surjective, in which we shall place ourselves in what follows. In this case, for every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the canonical homomorphism \[ F \longrightarrow p_*(p^*(F)) \] is injective. In case (i), to verify the injectivity of \(H^0(X,F) \to H^0(Y,h^*(F))\), we are reduced at once to the case where we replace \(F\) by \(p_*(\bar F)\) (where we set \(\bar F = p^*(F)\)). Now consider the commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ H^0(X, p_*(\bar F)) \ar[r] \ar[dd]_{\wr} & H^0(Y, h^*(p_*(\bar F))) \ar[d] \\ & H^0(Y, p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ H^0(\bar X, \bar F) \ar[r] & H^0(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F)) , } \] where the left-hand vertical arrow and the second right-hand vertical arrow are the canonical isomorphisms, the first right-hand vertical arrow coming from the base change homomorphism by \(h\). By hypothesis the second horizontal arrow is injective, which immediately implies that the same holds for the first, which proves the non-"resp." assertion of (i). For the "resp." asser- tion, one assumes that the second horizontal arrow is surjective; moreover, the base change homomorphism being a monomorphism by hypothesis, the same holds for the first right-hand vertical arrow, hence for the composite of the two right-hand vertical arrows. It follows at once that the first horizontal arrow is also surjective, which completes the proof of (i). To prove (ii), thanks to what precedes and 6.5 (i) we are reduced to proving the surjectivity of \(H^1(X,F) \to H^1(Y,h^*(F))\). Using 6.6 (ii) we are again reduced to proving it for \(F\) of the form \(p_*(\bar F)\), where \(\bar F\) is a sheaf of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups on \(\bar X\) (IX 1.6 (ii)). Writing the exact sequences for the \(H^1\), (variants of (3.2)) for the morphisms \(p\) and \(p_Y\), we find a homomorphism of non-commutative exact sequences: \[ \xymatrix{ H^1(X, p_*(\bar F)) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^1(\bar X, \bar F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^0(X, R^1 p_*(\bar F)) \ar[d] \\ H^1(Y, p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) \ar[r] & H^1(\bar Y, \bar h^*(\bar F)) \ar[r] & H^0(Y, R^1 p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))) , } \] where in each row the first arrow is injective and identifies the first term with the inverse image, by the second arrow, of the marked point of the third term. By hypothesis on \(\bar h\), the middle vertical arrow is bijective. On the other hand, the two extreme vertical arrows factor respectively through \(H^1(Y,h^*(p_*(\bar F)))\) and \(H^0(Y,h^*(R^1 p_*(\bar F)))\), by composing the homomorphisms \(H^i(X,-) \to H^i(Y,-)\) (for \(i = 1\) and \(i = 0\) respectively) and the homomorphisms deduced by applying \(H^i(Y,-)\) (for these same values of \(i\)) to the base change homomorphism \(h^*(p_*(\bar F)) \to p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) resp. \(h^*(R^1 p_*(\bar F)) \to R^1 p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\). Since the first of these arrows is an isomorphism by hypothesis, it follows that the first vertical arrow of the diagram above is identified with the homo- morphism \(H^1(X,-) \to H^1(Y,-)\) that we wish to study. To prove its bijec- tivity, it therefore remains to prove that the last vertical arrow of the diagram is injective. Now, by what we have just said, it is composed of two maps, of which the first is a canonical homomorphism \(H^0(X,-) \to H^0(Y,-)\), hence bijective, and the second is injective, since deduced by the left exact functor \(H^0(Y,-)\) from a homomorphism \(h^*(R^1 p_*(\bar F)) \to R^1 p_{Y*}(\bar h^*(\bar F))\) which is a monomorphism. This proves 6.8 (ii).

proposals.before: Suppose that \(\xi\) does not lie in the image of \(H^n(X,F)\). Let \(\Phi\) be the set of closed subsets \(X'\) of \(X\) such that the image of \(\xi\) in \(H^n(Y', h^*(F)|Y')\) is not contained in that of \(H^n(X', F|X')\). By hypothesis, \(X \in \Phi\), so \(\Phi\) is non-empty. Order \(\Phi\) by the relation \(\supset\), and let us show that \(\Phi\) is inductive. For this, it suffices to prove that if \((X'_\lambda)\) is a totally ordered family of elements of \(\Phi\), and if \(X'\) is their intersection, then \(X' \in \Phi\). Now, equip- ping the \(X'_\lambda\) and \(X'\) with the reduced induced structure, one sees that the morphisms \(X'_\lambda \to X\) are affine (since they are closed immersions), so the projective system of the \(X'_\lambda\) satisfies the conditions considered in VII 5. Moreover, one observes at once that \(X'\) is the projective limit of the \(X'_\lambda\). Likewise, \(Y'\) is the projective limit of the projective system of the \(Y'_\lambda\), which are affine over \(Y\). Using VII 5.8, we therefore find \[ \varinjlim H^n(X'_\lambda, F|X'_\lambda) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^n(X', F|X') , \quad \varinjlim H^n(Y'_\lambda, h^*(F)|Y'_\lambda) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^n(Y', h^*(F)|Y') . \] From this, one concludes at once that if one had \((\xi|Y') \in \operatorname{Im} H^n(X', F|X')\), then there would exist an index \(\lambda\) such that \((\xi|Y'_\lambda) \in \operatorname{Im} H^n(X'_\lambda, F|X'_\lambda)\), which is absurd; so one indeed has \(X' \in \Phi\). Hence \(\Phi\) is inductive, and consequently contains a minimal element, say \(X'\). Since evidently \(\emptyset \notin \Phi\), \(X'\) is non-empty. Remarks 6.13

The most important case where the conditions of 6.5 (i) (ii) (iii) are fulfilled is the one considered in 5.5, which will be proved in the following exposé using the reductions made in the present exposé. Another interesting case (where \(h\) is not a closed immersion as in 5.5) will be studied in XV. Let us also point out the case, fairly close to 5.5, where \(X\) is the spectrum of a noetherian ring, separated and complete for the topology defined by an ideal \(J\), and where \(Y = \operatorname{Spec}(A/J)\) is the closed subscheme of \(X\) defined by \(J\). One then verifies directly the conditions of 6.5 (ii) (with \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P}\)) in the form b'') (EGA IV 18.3.2); it is very plausible that the conditions of 6.5 (iii) are also verified for every \(n\), i.e. that for every sheaf of torsion \(F\) on \(X\), the homomorphisms \(H^n(X,F) \to H^n(Y,F|Y)\) are bijective. One can make considerably more general conjectures, connected with a generalization to non-local schemes of the henselization construction. First of all, let us note that no example is known, \(h\) being a closed immersion, where the conditions of 6.5 (ii) (iii) are not satisfied (with \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P}\)) when the "resp." condition of 6.5 (i) is, that is, when the pair \((X,Y)\) is a henselian pair in the terminology of (EGA IV 18.5.5); one may therefore conjecture that such a pair satisfies the conditions of 6.5 (ii) (iii) (with \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P}\), every \(n\)). On the other hand, one may ask under what conditions the following property for a pair \((X,Y)\) consisting of a quasi- complete and quasi-separated scheme \(X\) and a closed subscheme \(Y\) implies that the pair is henselian:

(*) For every scheme \(X'\) étale over \(X\), setting \(Y' = X' \times_X Y\), the canoni- cal map \(\Gamma(Y'/Y) \to \Gamma(X'/X)\) is bijective.

(Cf. EGA IV 18.5.4 b)). This condition is evidently a priori weaker than the henselian condition 6.5 (i); it is even strictly weaker, for it is verified for example if \(X\) is a normal irreducible projective scheme of dimension \(\geq 2\) over a field \(k\), and \(Y\) a hyperplane section of \(X\) (as follows easily from SGA 2 XII 2.1, where one takes \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\)), but evidently the pair \((X,Y)\) is not henselian. It is possible on the other hand that if \(X\) is affine, condition (*) implies that \((X,Y)\) is a henselian pair; if this were so, for every affine scheme \(X\) and every closed subset \(Y\) of \(X\), a process of étale localization along \(Y\), analogous to that of the hen- selization of local rings, should allow one to associate to it a henselian pair \((X',Y)\), where \(X'\) is "pro-étale" over \(X\). Another hypothesis on \((X,Y)\) (suggested by results of Hironaka and Rossi on the contractibility of certain subvarieties of algebraic varieties), which might perhaps allow one to deduce the henselian property from the weaker property (*), is the following: the immersion \(Y \to X\) is regular of codimension 1, and the conormal sheaf \(\underline{N}_{Y/X} = \underline{J}/\underline{J}^2\) (where \(\underline{J}\) is the ideal defining \(Y\) in \(X\)) is an ample invertible sheaf on \(Y\). (NB. In the case of the counterexample considered above, this conormal sheaf was on the contrary anti-ample, i.e. its inverse being ample).

Let us prove the theorem for all \(X\), by induction on \(n\): If the intersection \(U\) of the \(U_k\) is dense in \(X\) one may copy the proof of (EGA II 5.6, B, C, D), taking into account the modifica- tions of the notation. Using 6.1, we are reduced to the case of 5.5, with \(S\) strictly local. Let us now apply 6.10 taking \(Y = X_o\). Given \((\xi,X')\) as stated in 6.10, we apply Chow's lemma 7.1 to find an \(S\)-morphism \(p : \bar X \to X'\), with \(\bar X\) projective over \(S\), such that \(p(\bar X)\) contains a non-empty open subset of \(X'\) (condition 1°) of 6.10). proposals.before: Let us now show that to verify one of the three statements 5.1 for every situation \((f,F,g)\), with \(f\) projective, one may assume moreover that \(S\) is noetherian. For this, one notes that one may assume, thanks to 6.1, that \(S\) is strictly local and that \(S' \to S\) is the inclusion of the closed point, and one is reduced to verifying the statement 5.5 with \(S\) strictly local. Moreover, since \(X\) embeds in the standard projective scheme \(\mathbf{P}^r_S\), one may (thanks to the compati- bility 4.4 (ii)) replace \(X\) by \(\mathbf{P}^r_S\), \(F\) by its image in \(\mathbf{P}^r_S\), which brings us to the case where \(X = \mathbf{P}^r_S\). Note that \(A\) is the filtered inductive limit of noetherian henselian local subrings \(A_i\) such that the inclusion homomorphism \(A_i \to A\) is local: take the strict henselizations of the finite-type sub-\(\underline{\mathbb{Z}}\)-algebras of \(A\) at the prime ideals induced by the maximal ideal of \(A\). Under these conditions, the residue field \(k\) of \(A\) is also the inductive limit of the fields \(k\) of the \(A_i\) (EGA IV 5.13.1). Let \(S_i = \operatorname{Spec}(A_i)\), \(X_i = \mathbf{P}^r_{S_i}\), and suppose given an inductive system \((F_i)\) of sheaves of sets (resp. ...) on the \(X_i\) as in VII 5.7, and let \(F\) be the sheaf it defines on \(X\). Let \(F_{io}\) (resp. \(F_o\)) be the sheaf induced by \(F_i\) on the fibre \(X_{io}\) of the closed point \(s_i\) of \(S_i\) (resp. on the fibre \(X_o\) of the closed point \(s\) of \(S\)). Then one has a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \varinjlim_i H^n(X_i, F_i) \ar[r] \ar[d] & H^n(X, F) \ar[d] \\ \varinjlim_i H^n(X_{io}, F_{io}) \ar[r] & H^n(X_o, F_o) , } \] whose two horizontal arrows are isomorphisms, by virtue of VII 5.7. Consequently, to prove that the second vertical arrow is an isomorphism, it suffices to prove it for the first, so it suffices to prove that the homomorphisms \(H^n(X_i, F_i) \to H^n(X_{io}, F_{io})\) are isomorphisms. On the other hand, every sheaf of sets (resp. ...) \(F\) on \(X\) is isomorphic to the limit of an inductive system as above, taking for example \(F_i = u_{i*}(F)\), \(u_i : X \to X_i\) being the canonical morphism, by virtue of ( 5.2) and (IX 1.6 (iii)). This completes the proof of 8.1.

proposals.before: Indeed, we already know by 8.1 that one may restrict to the case \(f\) projective, \(S\) noetherian, and an argument already pointed out allows us to assume moreover that \(X = \mathbf{P}^r_S\). We then proceed by induction on \(r\), noting that the theorem is true by hypothesis for \(r = 1\). One may therefore assume \(r \geq 2\), and the theorem proved for \(\mathbf{P}^{r-1}_S \to S\) (every base \(S\)). Consider \(Z = \mathbf{P}^{r-2}_S\) as embedded in \(X = \mathbf{P}^r_S\) in the usual way, and let \(p : \bar X \to X\) be obtained by blowing up \(Z\) in \(X\). An immediate computation (cf. Remark 2.4

One can avoid recourse to the delicate result of SGA IX and to descent theory, by a direct argument, showing that the category of étale coverings of \(Z\) is equivalent to the category of triples \((X', Y', \theta)\), where \(X'(Y')\) is an étale covering of \(X(Y)\) and \(\theta\) a \(V\)-isomorphism \(X' \times_X V \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} Y' \times_Y V\). Definition 1.3

A morphism \(g : X \to Y\) having one of the equivalent properties (i) to (iii) (resp. (i) to (iii) in the resp. sense) of 1.1 is called a \((-1)\)-acyclic (resp. \(0\)-acyclic) morphism. Proposition 1.5

Soient \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\) deux univers, \(C\) et \(C'\) deux \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites, \(u : C \to C'\) un foncteur entre les catégories sous-jacentes. Alors \(u\) est continu rela- tivement à \(\mathcal{U}\) si et seulement s'il est continu relativement à \(\mathcal{V}\). De plus, lorsque \(u\) est continu, désignons par \(u^s_{\mathcal{U}}\) (resp. \(u^s_{\mathcal{V}}\)) le foncteur entre catégories de \(\mathcal{U}\)-faisceaux (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)-faisceaux) introduit en 1.2 iv). Alors le diagramme \[ (1.5.1) \qquad \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[r]^-{u^s_{\mathcal{U}}} \ar[d] & \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[d] \\ \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}} \ar[r]_-{u^s_{\mathcal{V}}} & \widetilde{C}'_{\mathcal{V}} , } \] où les foncteurs verticaux sont les foncteurs d'inclusion canoniques, est commutatif à isomorphisme canonique près.

Proposition 1.6

Soient \(C\) et \(C'\) deux \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites, \(u : C \to C'\) un foncteur entre les catégories sous-jacentes. Considérons les conditions :

  1. i)

    \(u\) est continu (cf. 1.1 et 1.2).

  2. ii)

    Pour toute famille couvrante \((X_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), de \(C\), la famille \((u X_i \to u X)\), \(i \in I\), de \(C'\), est couvrante.

On a l'implication i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii).

Supposons que la topologie de \(C\) puisse être définie par une prétopologie \(T\) (II 1.3) et que le foncteur \(u\) commute aux produits fibrés.(∗) Alors les conditions i) et ii) sont équivalentes et sont équivalentes à la con- dition suivante :

  1. iii)

    Le foncteur \(u\) transforme les familles couvrantes de \(T\) en familles couvrantes de \(C'\).

En particulier, supposons que dans \(C\) les produits fibrés soient représentables et que le foncteur \(u\) commute aux produits fibrés. Alors les conditions i) et ii) sont équivalentes.

proposals.before: Toute famille couvrante de la prétopologie \(T\) est une famille couvrante de \(C\), d'où ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) iii). Montrons que iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). Soit \(X\) un objet de \(C\) et \(X_i \to X\), \(i \in I\), une famille couvrante de \(\mathrm{Cov}(X)\) (II 1.3). Les morphismes \(X_i \to X\) sont quarrables et le foncteur \(u\) commute aux produits fibrés. Par suite, les produits fibrés \(u(X_i) \times_{u(X)} u(X_j)\) sont représentables et canoniquement isomorphes à \(u(X_i \times_X X_j)\). Soit \(F\) un faisceau sur \(C'\). Alors le diagramme d'ensembles : \[ F(u(X)) \longrightarrow \prod_i F(u(X_i)) \rightrightarrows \prod_{i,j} F(u(X_i \times_X X_j)) \] est exact (II 2.1, I 3.5 et I 2.12). Par suite le diagramme d'ensembles \[ u^* F(X) \longrightarrow \prod_i u^* F(X_i) \rightrightarrows \prod_{i,j} u^* F(X_i \times_X X_j) \] est exact. Donc \(u^* F\) est un faisceau (II 2.4), d'où i). La dernière asser- tion de 1.6 résulte de ce qui précède et du fait que, lorsque les produits fibrés sont représentables dans \(C\), toutes les familles couvrantes de \(C\)(1) définissent sur \(C\) une prétopologie dont la topologie associée est la topologie de \(C\).

Notation 1.8

Nous emploierons dorénavant la notation \(u_s\) pour désigner le foncteur \(u_s^\gamma\). Cette notation ne risque pas d'apporter de confusion, car le foncteur \(u_s\) (défini sur les faisceaux d'ensembles) commute aux limites projectives finies.

De même, lorsque \(u^s\) est exact à gauche, nous emploierons la notation \(u^s\) pour désigner le foncteur \(u^s_\gamma\). Cet abus de notation est jus- tifié par 1.7 4).

Exemple 1.9.1

Soit \(X\) un petit espace topologique. Désignons par \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) la catégorie des ouverts de \(X\) (les objets de \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) sont les sous-ensembles ouverts de \(X\), les morphismes de \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) sont les inclusions) munie de la topologie canonique. Une famille \((U_i \subset U)\), \(i \in I\), est couvrante si et seu- lement si les ouverts \(U_i\) recouvrent \(U\) (II 2.6). Les faisceaux d'ensem- bles sur \(\mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) sont donc les faisceaux d'ensembles au sens de [TF]. Soit \(f : X \to Y\) une application continue. On en déduit un foncteur \(f^{-1} : \mathrm{Ouv}(Y) \to \mathrm{Ouv}(X)\) : pour tout ouvert \(U\) de \(Y\), \(f^{-1}(U)\) est l'image réciproque de \(U\) par l'application \(f\). Le foncteur \(f^{-1}\) est un foncteur continu (1.6). Le foncteur \(f^{-1}_s : \mathrm{Ouv}(X)^{\sim} \to \mathrm{Ouv}(Y)^{\sim}\) est le foncteur image directe pour les faisceaux, au sens de [TF]. Le foncteur \((f^{-1})^s : \mathrm{Ouv}(Y)^{\sim} \to \mathrm{Ouv}(X)^{\sim}\) est le foncteur image réciproque pour les faisceaux au sens de [TF]. Le foncteur \((f^{-1})^s\) commute aux limites projectives finies, grâce à 1.3 5).

proposals.before:
Exemple 1.9.3

Soient \(C\) et \(C'\) deux petits sites, \(u : C \to C'\) un foncteur entre les catégories sous-jacentes qui transforme toute famille couvrante de \(C\) en famille couvrante de \(C'\). Le foncteur \(u\) n'est pas continu en général (cf. cependant 1.6). Voici un contre-exemple. Soit \(S\) un ensemble de cardinal infini de l'univers \(\mathcal{U}\), et \(C\) la sous-catégorie pleine de la catégorie des ensembles, dont les objets sont les sous-ensembles finis, non-vides, de \(S\). On munit \(C\) de la topologie canonique. On remarquera que les familles couvrantes de \(C\) sont les familles surjectives d'applications et que les familles couvrantes ne sont pas vides. On remarquera de plus qu'il n'y a, à isomorphisme près, que deux faisceaux constants sur \(C\) : le faisceau de valeur l'ensemble vide et le faisceau de valeur l'ensemble à un élément. Posons \(C = C'\) et soit \(u : C \to C'\) un foncteur constant. Le foncteur \(u\) transforme les familles couvrantes de \(C\) en familles couvrantes de \(C'\). Le foncteur \(u\) n'est pas continu. En effet, comme les préfaisceaux représen- tables de \(C'\) sont des faisceaux, pour tout objet \(X\) de \(C'\), il existe un faisceau \(F\) sur \(C'\) tel que le cardinal de l'ensemble \(F(X)\) soit \(\geq 2\), et par suite le préfaisceau \(u^* F\) n'est pas un faisceau.

Posons \(C = C'\) et soit \(u : C \to C'\) un foncteur constant. Le foncteur \(u\) transforme les familles couvrantes de \(C\) en familles couvrantes de \(C'\). Le foncteur \(u\) n'est pas continu. En effet, comme les préfaisceaux représentables de \(C'\) sont des faisceaux, pour tout objet \(X\) de \(C'\), il existe un faisceau \(F\) sur \(C'\) tel que le cardinal de l'ensemble \(F(X)\) soit \(\geq 2\), et par suite le préfaisceau \(u^* F\) n'est pas un faisceau.

proposals.before: Preuve. La condition est suffisante. Supposons que pour tout faisceau \(G\) sur \(C\), le préfaisceau \(\widehat{u}_* G\) soit un faisceau. Soient \(Y\) un objet de \(C\) et \(R \hookrightarrow u(Y)\) un crible couvrant. On a un isomorphisme \(\mathrm{Hom}(u(Y), \widehat{u}_* G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(R, \widehat{u}_* G)\), d'où par adjonction (I 5.1) un iso- morphisme \(\mathrm{Hom}(\widehat{u}^* \circ u(Y), G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(\widehat{u}^* R, G)\). On en déduit (II 5.3) que le morphisme \(\widehat{u}^* R \to \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) est bicouvrant. Mais le foncteur \(\widehat{u}^*\) commute aux limites projectives et par suite le morphisme \(\widehat{u}^* R \to \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) est un monomorphisme. C'est donc un monomorphisme couvrant. D'autre part on a un morphisme canonique \(Y \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\) déduit du morphisme d'adjonction \(\mathrm{id}_C \to \widehat{u}^* u\), (I 5.4 3)). Faisons alors le changement de base \(Y \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \widehat{u}^* u(Y)\). On obtient un crible couvrant \(Y\) : \[ \widehat{u}^* R \times_{\widehat{u}^* u(Y)} Y \longrightarrow Y , \] et lorsqu'on cherche les flèches \(Z \to Y\) qui se factorisent par ce crible, on obtient le crible décrit par la propriété (COC).

proposals.before: Soit \(C/H\) la petite catégorie dont les objets sont les objets \(Y\) de \(C\) muni d'un morphisme \(u(Y) \to H\), et dont les morphismes sont les diagrammes commutatifs : \[ \xymatrix{ u(Y) \ar[rr]^-{u(m)} \ar[dr] & & u(Y') \ar[dl] \\ & H & } \] On a \(u^* H = \varinjlim_{Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, C/H} Y\) (I 3.4) et par suite (I 5.4) \(u_! u^* H = \varinjlim_{Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, C/H} u(Y)\). Le morphisme d'adjonction est le morphisme évident qui résulte de la description de \(u_! u^* H\) comme limite inductive. Le morphisme \(\varphi\) possède la propriété suivante : (∗) Pour tout objet \(Y\) de \(C\), tout morphisme \(m : u(Y) \to H\) se factorise de manière unique en le morphisme canonique \(\alpha(m) : u(Y) \to u_! u^* H\) et le morphisme \(\varphi\). Il résulte immédiatement de i) que le morphisme \(\varphi\) est couvrant (II 5.1), montrons qu'il est bicouvrant. Soient \(p, q : Z \rightrightarrows u_! u^* H\) deux morphismes d'un objet \(Z\) de \(\widehat{C}'\), tels que \(\varphi p = \varphi q\). Pour tout objet \(Y\) de \(C\) et tout morphisme \(n : u(Y) \to Z\), on a \(\varphi p n = \varphi q n\). La propriété (∗) entraîne alors que \(p n = q n\), et comme les \(u(Y)\) recouvrent \(Z\), le noyau de \((p, q)\) est un crible couvrant \(Z\). Le mor- phisme \(\varphi\) est donc bicouvrant (II 5.3). Pour tout faisceau \(H\) sur \(C'\), \(u^* H\) est un faisceau sur \(C\) noté \(u_s H\) (1.1.1). On a de plus \(u^s u_s H = a' u_! u_s H\) (1.3), et le morphisme d'adjonction \(u^s u_s H \to H\) s'obtient en appliquant le foncteur « faisceau associé » au morphisme \(\varphi : u_! u^* H \to H\). Par suite (II 5.3) le morphisme d'adjonction \(u^s u_s H \to H\) est un isomorphisme. Donc \(u_s : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) est pleinement fidèle.

Le morphisme d'adjonction est le morphisme évident qui résulte de la description de \(u_! u^* H\) comme limite inductive. Le morphisme \(\varphi\) possède la propriété suivante : (∗) Pour tout objet \(Y\) de \(C\), tout morphisme \(m : u(Y) \to H\) se factorise de manière unique en le morphisme canonique \(\alpha(m) : u(Y) \to u_! u^* H\) et le morphisme \(\varphi\). Il résulte immédiatement de i) que le morphisme \(\varphi\) est couvrant (II 5.1), montrons qu'il est bicouvrant. Soient \(p, q : Z \rightrightarrows u_! u^* H\) deux morphismes d'un objet \(Z\) de \(\widehat{C}'\), tels que \(\varphi p = \varphi q\). Pour tout objet \(Y\) de \(C\) et tout morphisme \(n : u(Y) \to Z\), on a \(\varphi p n = \varphi q n\). La propriété (∗) entraîne alors que \(p n = q n\), et comme les \(u(Y)\) recouvrent \(Z\), le noyau de \((p, q)\) est un crible couvrant \(Z\). Le morphisme \(\varphi\) est donc bicouvrant (II 5.3). Pour tout faisceau \(H\) sur \(C'\), \(u^* H\) est un faisceau sur \(C\) noté \(u_s H\) (1.1.1). On a de plus \(u^s u_s H = a' u_! u_s H\) (1.3), et le morphisme d'adjonction \(u^s u_s H \to H\) s'obtient en appliquant le foncteur « faisceau associé » au morphisme \(\varphi : u_! u^* H \to H\). Par suite (II 5.3) le morphisme d'adjonction \(u^s u_s H \to H\) est un isomorphisme. Donc \(u_s : \widetilde{C}' \to \widetilde{C}\) est pleinement fidèle.

Proposition 5.5

1) Soient \(C\) un \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(X\) un objet de \(\widehat{C}\). Le diagramme ci-dessous de catégories et foncteurs est commutatif à isomorphismes canoniques près : \[ \xymatrix@C=2.6em{ C/X \ar[r]^-{h_X} \ar@{=}[d] & (C/X)^{\wedge} \ar[r]^-{a_X} \ar[d]^-{e_X^{\wedge}} & (C/X)^{\sim} \ar[r]^-{i_X} \ar[d]^-{e_X^{\sim}} & (C/X)^{\wedge} \ar[d]^-{e^{\wedge}/X} & \\ C/X \ar[r]_-{h/X} & \widehat{C}/X \ar[r]_-{a/X} & \widetilde{C}/aX \ar[r]_-{i/aX} & \widehat{C}/iaX \ar[r]_-{\pi} & \widehat{C}/X . } \] Les notations \(a_X\) et \(i_X\) désignent les foncteurs « faisceau associé » et injection dans les préfaisceaux pour le site \(C/X\). La nota- tion \(a/X\) désigne le prolongement naturel du foncteur \(a\) (faisceau asso- cié pour le site \(C\)) à la catégorie des flèches de but \(X\), de même pour la notation \(i/aX\). Enfin la notation \(\pi\) désigne le foncteur changement de base par la flèche canonique \(X \to iaX\).

2) Soit de plus \(m : Y \to X\) un morphisme de \(\widehat{C}\). Le diagramme ci-après est commutatif à isomorphisme canonique près : \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \widetilde{C}/aX/aY \ar@{=}[dd] & & (C/X)^{\sim}/a_X Y \ar[ll]_-{f} \ar[dr]^-{g} & \\ & & & (C/X/Y)^{\sim} \ar[dl]^-{e_m^{\sim}} \\ \widetilde{C}/aY & & (C/Y)^{\sim} \ar[ll]^-{e_Y^{\sim}} & } \]

La flèche \(f\) est le prolongement naturel de l'équivalence \(e^{\sim}/X\) à la catégorie des flèches de but \(a_X Y\), et est par suite une équi- valence de catégories. La flèche \(g\) n'est autre que l'équivalence de 5.4 appliquée à la situation \((C/X)/[m]\).

3) Désignons par \(j_{aX!} : \widetilde{C}/aX \to \widetilde{C}\) le foncteur « oublions \(aX\) », et par \(j_{aX}^* : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}/aX\) le foncteur « produit par \(aX\) ». Les diagrammes ci-après sont commutatifs à isomorphisme canonique près : \[ \xymatrix{ (C/X)^{\sim} \ar[r]^-{j_{X!}} \ar[d] & \widetilde{C} \ar@{=}[d] \\ \widetilde{C}/aX \ar[r]_-{j_{aX!}} & \widetilde{C} } \qquad \xymatrix{ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]^-{j_X^*} \ar@{=}[d] & (C/X)^{\sim} \ar[d]^-{e^{\sim}/X} \\ \widetilde{C} \ar[r]_-{j_{aX}^*} & \widetilde{C}/aX } \]

Définition 1.1

Soit \(p\) un ensemble de nombres premiers. On dit que \(F\) est un faisceau de \(p\)-torsion, où un \(p\)-faisceau, si le morphisme canonique \[ \varinjlim_n {}_n F \longrightarrow F \quad \text{est bijectif} , \] \(n\) parcourant l'ensemble des entiers tels que ass \(n \subset p\), c'est-à-dire, tels que les nombres premiers divisant \(n\) soient dans \(p\). (i) \(F\) est de \(p\)-torsion si et seulement si \(F\) est le faisceau associé à un préfaisceau à valeurs dans des groupes abéliens de \(p\)-torsion; on peut prendre \[ P = \varinjlim_{\text{ass } n \subset p}^{(\text{préf})} {}_n F . \]

(ii) Si \(F\) est de \(p\)-torsion et si \(X \in \operatorname{Ob} T\) est un objet quasi-compact(∗), alors \(F(X)\) est un groupe de \(p\)-torsion.

(iii) Si \(T\) est localement de type fini (VI 1.1), alors \(F\) est de \(p\)-torsion si et seulement si \(F(X)\) est un groupe de \(p\)-torsion pour chaque \(X \in \operatorname{Ob} T\) quasi-compact. Dans ce cas, on a \[ \varinjlim_{\text{ass } n \subset p} H^q(T/X; {}_n F) \xrightarrow{\sim} H^q(T/X; F) \] pour chaque \(X\) quasi-compact et tout \(q\).

(iv) Si \(u : T \to T'\) est un morphisme de topos et si \(F'\) est de \(p\)-torsion sur \(T'\), alors l'image inverse \(u^* F'\) est un faisceau de \(p\)-torsion sur \(T\).

(v) Si \(u : T \to T'\) est un morphisme de topos, avec \(T\) et \(T'\) localement de type fini et \(u\) quasi-compact(∗), et si \(F\) est un faisceau de \(p\)-torsion sur \(T\), alors les \(R^q u_* F'\) sont des faisceaux de \(p\)-torsion sur \(T\) pour tout \(q\).

proposals.before: Démonstration. (i) Supposons que \(F\) soit un faisceau de ind-\(p\)-groupes, et soit \(\xi\) un point géométrique de \(X\). Alors \(F = \varinjlim F(X')\), où \(X'\) parcourt un système pseudo-filtrant de schémas étales sur \(X\) (VIII 3.9). Il est évident que les \(X'\) affines (donc quasi-compacts) forment un ensemble cofinal, et que par suite \(F\) est limite inductive de ind \(p\)-groupes, donc est un ind-\(p\)-groupe d'après 1.4 (ii). Inversement, supposons que pour chaque \(\xi\) la fibre \(F_\xi\) soit un ind-\(p\)-groupe et soit \(U \longrightarrow X\) étale, \(U\) quasi-compact. Soit \(S \subset F(U)\) un sous-ensemble fini. Pour chaque point géométrique \(\xi\) de \(U\), l'image de \(S\) dans \(F_\xi\) engendre un groupe fini. Comme un groupe fini est de présentation finie, on conclut aisément qu'il existe un \(U_\xi\) étale sur \(U\), \(\xi\)-ponctué, tel que \(S\) engendre un groupe fini dans \(F(U_\xi)\) (cf. VIII 4). Un nombre fini de tels \(U_\xi\) forment un recouvrement de \(U\), soit \(\{ U_1, \ldots, U_n \}\). Alors l'image de \(S\) dans \(\prod F(U_i)\) engendre un sous-groupe fini, et comme \(F(U) \subset \prod F(U_i)\), on a gagné.

proposals.before: Supposons que \(F\) soit un faisceau d'ensembles constructibles. Utilisant l'existence des sommes infinies dans le site étale sur \(X\), on voit que l'on peut trouver un épimorphisme \(G \to F\), avec \(G\) représentable par un schéma étale sur \(X\), que l'on peut de plus supposer somme de schémas affines \(G_i\) (\(i \in I\)), donc séparé sur \(S\). Pour toute partie finie \(J\) de l'ensemble d'in- dices \(I\), soit \(G_J\) la somme des \(G_i\) pour \(i \in J\), \(F_J\) son image dans \(F\). Comme \(G_J\) et \(F\) sont constructibles, il en est de même de \(F_J\) (2.6 (ibis)), donc l'ensemble \(X_J\) des \(x \in X\) tels que les fibres de \(F\) et \(F_J\) en un point géométrique de \(X\) sur \(x\) soient égales, est localement constructible 2.4 (iv). Comme la famille des \(X_J\) est croissante et de réunion \(X\), et que \(X\) est quasi-compact, l'un des \(X_J\) est égal à \(X\) (EGA IV 1.9.9). Cela montre, quitte à remplacer \(G\) par \(G_J\), que l'on peut supposer \(G\) affine, donc séparé sur \(S\), et quasi-compact sur \(X\) puisque \(X\) est quasi-séparé (EGA IV 1.2.4). Soit alors \(H = G \times_X G\). C'est un sous-faisceau de \(G \times_S G\) qui est représentable, donc est lui-même représentable (VIII 6.1). Comme \(G\) est de plus constructible (2.6 (ibis)), il résulte encore de l'argument précédent qu'il est quasi-compact, donc (étant séparé sur \(X\)) de présentation finie sur \(X\). Cela prouve la pre- mière assertion de 2.7, et la deuxième se prouve par la même méthode (NB il n'est pas nécessaire que \(A\) soit noethérien). proposals.before:
Proposition 0.5

Soient \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\) deux univers, \(\mathcal{A}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{B}\)) une \(\mathcal{U}\)-catégorie (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)-catégorie) abélienne vérifiant l'axiome AB 5) relativement à \(\mathcal{U}\) (resp. à \(\mathcal{V}\)) et possédant une famille génératrice \(\mathcal{U}\)-petite (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)-petite). Soit \(\varepsilon : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{B}\) un foncteur exact et pleinement fidèle. Les conditions suivantes sont équivalentes :

  1. 1)

    Il existe une famille génératrice \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) de \(\mathcal{A}\) telle la famille \((\varepsilon(X_i))_{i \in I}\) soit génératrice dans \(\mathcal{B}\).

  2. 1')

    Tout objet de \(\mathcal{B}\) est isomorphe à un quotient d'un objet du type \(\bigoplus_{\alpha \in A} \varepsilon(Y_\alpha)\) où \(A \in \mathcal{V}\).

Sous ces conditions, on a la propriété suivante :

  1. 2)

    \(\varepsilon\) transforme les produits \(\mathcal{U}\)-petits en produits (donc commute aux limites projectives \(\mathcal{U}\)-petites).

De plus, sous les conditions équivalentes 1) ou 1'), les conditions suivantes sont équivalentes :

  1. a)

    Pour tout objet \(Y\) de \(\mathcal{A}\), tout sous-objet de \(\varepsilon(Y)\) est isomorphe à l'image par \(\varepsilon\) d'un sous-objet de \(Y\).

  2. a')

    Il existe une famille génératrice \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) de \(\mathcal{A}\) telle que la famille \((\varepsilon(X_i))_{i \in I}\) soit génératrice dans \(\mathcal{B}\) et telle que pour tout \(i \in I\), tout sous-objet de \(\varepsilon(X_i)\) soit isomorphe à l'image par \(\varepsilon\) d'un sous-objet de \(X_i\).

  3. b)

    Tout objet de \(\mathcal{B}\) est isomorphe à un sous-objet d'un objet du type \(\prod_{\alpha \in A} \varepsilon(Y_\alpha)\) où \(A \in \mathcal{V}\).

  4. c)

    \(\varepsilon\) commute aux sommes directes \(\mathcal{U}\)-petites (donc commute aux limites inductives \(\mathcal{U}\)-petites).

De plus, sous les conditions 1) et a') on a :

  1. d)

    \(\varepsilon\) transforme les objets injectifs en objets injectifs.

Théorème 1.1

Soit \(f : X' \to X\) un morphisme entier surjectif radiciel. Alors le foncteur changement de base \[ f^* : X_{\text{ét}} \to X'_{\text{ét}} \] est une équivalence de sites (i.e. une équivalence de catégorie, qui est continue ainsi que tout foncteur quasi-inverse). Par suite les foncteurs \[ f_* : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X'}_{\text{ét}} \] \[ f^* : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X'}_{\text{ét}} \] sont des équivalences de catégories, quasi-inverses l'une de l'autre.

proposals.before: La première assertion est bien connue (SGA IX 4.10 et 4.11) lorsque \(f\) est de présentation finie ou que \(f\) est plat; le cas général se réduit à celui où \(f\) est de présentation finie. En effet, on sait déjà que le foncteur \(f^*\) est pleinement fidèle (SGA 1 IX 3.4). Il suffit de prouver que \(f^*\) est essentiellement surjectif, i.e. que tout \(Z'\) étale sur \(X'\) "provient" d'un \(Z\) étale sur \(X\). Utilisant le fait que \(f\) est un homéomorphisme universel, et la pleine fidélité de \(f^*\), on est ramené au cas où \(X\), \(X'\), \(Z'\) sont affines, spectres d'anneaux \(A\), \(A'\), \(B'\). Ecrivant \(A'\) comme limite inductive de ses sous-\(A\)-algèbres de type fini \(A'_i\), \(B'\) provient d'une algèbre étale \(B'_i\) sur un \(A'_i\) (cf. EGA IV 8), ce qui nous ramène au cas où \(A'\) est entière et de type fini sur \(A\), donc finie sur \(A\). On a alors un \(A\) isomorphisme \(A' \simeq A''/J\), ou \(A'' \simeq A[t_1, \ldots t_n]\) et \(J\) est un idéal de \(A''\). Ecrivant \(J\) comme limite inductive de ses sous-idéaux \(J_i\) de type fini, et posant \(A'_i = A''/J_i\), on aura encore \(A' = \varinjlim_i A'_i\), donc \(B'\) provient d'une algèbre étale \(B'_i\) sur un \(A'_i\) (loco citato). D'autre part, comme \(\operatorname{Spec} A' \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) est surjectif, il en est de même \(\operatorname{Spec} A'_i \to \operatorname{Spec} A\), et de plus on vérifie facilement que puisque \(\operatorname{Spec} A' \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) est radiciel, il en est de même de \(\operatorname{Spec} A'_i \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) pour \(i\) assez grand (appliquer EGA IV 1.9.9 à \(\operatorname{Spec} A\)(∗)). Cela nous ramène au cas où \(A'\) est un des \(A'_i\), donc de présentation finie sur \(A\).

proposals.before: En effet, notons d'abord que pour tout préfaisceau \(P\) sur \(\xi_{\text{ét}}\), si \(aP\) est le faisceau associé, l'homomorphisme naturel \[ P(\xi) \to aP(\xi) \] est un isomorphisme, comme il résulte par exemple aussitôt du calcul explicite de \(aP\) comme \(L(LP)\) (II 3.19.). Soit \(\varphi : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{\xi}_{\text{ét}}\) le foncteur "image réciproque", alors \(u^* = \varphi^*\) n'est autre (III 2.3.(d)) que le composé \(a\, \varphi'\, i\), où \(i : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widehat{X}_{\text{ét}}\) est le foncteur inclusion, et \(a : \widehat{\xi}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{\xi}_{\text{ét}}\) le foncteur "faisceau associé". Par la remarque précédente on trouve \[ u^*(F)(\xi) = (\varphi'i(F))(\xi) , \] de sorte qu'il suffit d'appliquer l'expression explicite de \(\varphi'\) donnée dans la démonstration de . Le cas resp., où on part avec un préfaisceau \(P\) sur \(X\), se prouve de même, en utilisant l'isomorphisme fonctoriel \(\varphi^*a(P) \simeq a \varphi(P)\) . Le fait que la catégorie \(C_\xi\) est filtrante (qui reste valable pour tout \(X\)-schéma \(\xi\), pas nécessairement réduit à un point géométrique) résulte aussitôt du fait que dans \(C_\xi\) les limites projectives finies existent, ce qui résulte du fait que \(X_{\text{ét}}\) est une sous-catégorie de \((\mathrm{Sch})_{/X}\) stable par limites projectives finies.

proposals.before: Prenons par exemple le cas d'une variété \(X\) algébrique irré- ductible, de dimension \(n\), sur un corps séparablement clos \(k\), et fi- xons \(\ell \neq \operatorname{car} k\). Un théorème qu'on trouvera dans le n° 4 donne pour la dimension cohomologique la majoration \(2n\), qui est la dimension "véri- table" de \(X\) (suggérée par l'analogie topologique dans le cas où \(k = \mathbb{C}\)). Ce résultat est assez élémentaire à partir de la théorie pour les corps, et en fait la majoration par \(2n\) peut être améliorée sauf dans le cas où \(X\) est complète : il existe une autre majoration, \(2n-1\), qui est vraie chaque fois que dans \(X\) il "manque au moins un point". Cette dernière majoration est la bonne "majoration stable", dans le sens que chaque \(X\) de dimension \(n\) contient un ouvert de dimension coho- mologique \(2n-1\). Une troisième majoration est obtenue pour une variété affine, où on obtient \(n\) comme dimension cohomologique. C'est une géné- ralisation d'un des théorèmes de Lefschetz pour les sections hyperplanes. Ces deux dernières assertions sont plus profondes et ne pourront être démontrées que plus tard (XIV).

proposals.before: Démonstration. Cela veut dire que le foncteur \(L \longmapsto \hat{L} = L \otimes_K \hat{K}\) de la catégorie des \(K\)-algèbres étales dans la catégorie des \(\hat{K}\)-algèbres étales est une équivalence. Or chaque algèbre étale \(\hat{K}'\) de \(\hat{K}\) est induite par une algèbre étale convenable \(K'\) de \(K\). En effet, si \(\hat{K}' = \hat{K}[\alpha]\) où \(\alpha\) satisfait à l'équation irréductible séparable \(f(T) = 0\) à coefficients dans \(\hat{R}\), il suffit de prendre pour \(K'\) l'algèbre \(K[\alpha_0]\), où \(\alpha_0\) est racine d'une équation \(f_0(T) = 0\) à coefficients dans \(R\) avec \(f_0 \equiv f \ (\hat{\mathfrak{m}}^N)\), \(N\) grand et \(\hat{\mathfrak{m}}\) l'idéal maximal de \(\hat{R}\). C'est l'application de la "méthode de Newton" habituelle (Bourbaki, Alg. Comm. III 4.5). Il reste à démontrer que le foncteur est pleine- ment fidèle (il est évidemment fidèle), et il revient au même de démon- trer que si \(K'\) est un corps, il en est de même de \(\hat{K}'\). Soit \(R'\) le normalisé de \(R\) dans \(K'\), qui est fini sur \(R\) puisque \(K'/K\) est sé- parable. L'anneau \(R'\) est un anneau de valuation discrète, et le complété de \(R'\) est \(\hat{R}' = R' \otimes_R \hat{R}\). Donc \(\hat{R}'\) est un anneau de valua- tion discrète, et comme \(\hat{K}'\) en est l'anneau total des fractions, il est bien un corps.

proposals.before: Démonstration. On peut supposer \(A\) intègre, à corps des fractions \(R(A) = K\). Soit \(x \in \mathfrak{r}A\) un élément qui n'est pas diviseur de zéro. Alors \(\dim A/(x) = \dim A - 1\). Par récurrence sur \(\dim A\), on a \[ \operatorname{cd}_\ell R(A/(x)) \geqslant \operatorname{cd}_\ell k + \dim A - 1 . \] Soit \(k'\) un corps résiduel de \(R(A/(x))\) tel que \(\operatorname{cd}_\ell k' = \operatorname{cd}_\ell R(A/(x))\) (cf VIII 1), et soit \(P\) l'idéal premier, noyau de \(A \longrightarrow k'\). L'anneau \(A_P\) est de dimension 1. Il suffit donc de démontrer le corollaire pour l'an- neau local \(A_P\), c'est-à-dire, on est réduit au cas où \(\dim A = 1\). Soit \(\widetilde{A}\) le hensélisé de \(A\). Chaque corps résiduel de \(R(\widetilde{A})\) s'identifie à une extension séparable de \(R(\widetilde{A}) = K\), et on a donc \[ \operatorname{cd}_\ell R(A) = \operatorname{cd}_\ell K \geqslant \operatorname{cd}_\ell R(\widetilde{A}) . \] On est ainsi ramené au cas où \(A\) est de dimension 1 et hensélien, ce qui est conséquence de 2.3.

proposals.before: Ecrivons \(A = \varinjlim B_\alpha\) où les \(B_\alpha\) sont des anneaux de type fini sur \(\mathbb{Z}\). Le morphisme \(B_\alpha \to A\) se factorise par le hensélisé \(A_\alpha\) de \(B_\alpha\) en l'idéal premier induit par \(\operatorname{rad} A\), d'où \(A = \varinjlim A_\alpha\). On constate aisément qu'on a aussi \(A\{t\} = \varinjlim A_\alpha\{t\}\). De plus, soient \(\bar{y}\) un point géométrique de \(\operatorname{Spec} A\), \(X_{\bar{y}}\) la fibre géométrique de \(S = \operatorname{Spec} A\{t\}\) sur \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) en \(\bar{y}\), \(\bar{y}_\alpha\) le point de \(\operatorname{Spec} A_\alpha\) induit par \(\bar{y}\), et \(X_{\alpha\,\bar{y}_\alpha}\) la fibre géométrique de \(\operatorname{Spec} A_\alpha\{t\}\) sur \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) en \(\bar{y}_\alpha\). On a \(X_{\bar{y}} = \varprojlim X_{\alpha\,\bar{y}_\alpha}\). On est donc réduit pour la démonstration de 2.5 par 1.7 (ii) (appliqué aux morphismes \(X_{\alpha\,\bar{y}_\alpha} \to \bar{y}_\alpha\)) au cas \(A = A_\alpha\), c'est-à-dire, où \(A\) est le hensélisé d'une algèbre de type fini sur \(\mathbb{Z}\) en un idéal premier donné. Nous les supposons désormais. Rappelons qu'une telle algèbre est un anneau excellent (EGA IV 7.8.3 (iii), 7.8.6 (i)), donc que \(A_\alpha\) est également excellent (comme on voit facilement sur la définition, cf. EGA IV 18.7.6).
